steps: Select the location
Plan room for the hearth extension, mantel, heat and combustion-air ducting; avoid cutting joists or rafters. An interior chimney drafts best.

Consider windows, doors, adjacent side walls and traffic flow, leaving space in front for the hearth extension and mantel. Plan hot air ducts, heat circulation and combustion air ducting. Avoid cutting floor joists or rafters where possible.

In most cases no additional floor support is needed for the unit and facing; confirm with local code or a structural engineer.

In areas below 0° Fahrenheit an exterior chimney raises the risk of poor draft, creosote and slow starts. Low installs (basement) with an outside chimney are especially prone to flow reversal on start up.
Platform, framing & chase
Build any raised-hearth platform; frame the chase and cut openings for air supply, chimney, heat dump kit and top vents. Insulate now; sheet rock must cover insulated walls.

Finished frame opening45 1/2" W x 51" H x 24" D min
Top vent frame opening12" W x 18 1/4" H each
Interior chase width55" recommended

Protect a raised combustible hearth structure with the Micore provided. Don't create the finished frame opening before the unit is in place, or it won't fit past the combustion air connection. Sheet rock over insulated walls prevents sagging and contact with the unit.
Outside air & set the unit
Install the outside air assembly in the chase, move the fireplace into place and connect the air supply at its lower left.

Insulated class 1 duct, 4" min; beyond ten feet use 6" reduced to 4" at the unit; 25' and three 90 degree bends max. Terminate outdoors with the screened vent, never in an attic or garage, and form an "S" trap. Mobile homes: standard kit only, and bolt the unit to the floor through the two side clips.
Install the chimney
8" UL-103HT, one brand, per the chimney maker. Fix the brand's anchor plate with 4 self tapping metal screws and seal it with 600 degree RTV silicone.

Firestop and/or radiation shield at combustible penetrations, sealed storm collar at the flashing, roof support, and a chimney cap. Total height 15' to 36' from unit base to cap; the unit supports 12'. Max offset 30 degree, no more than two sets of elbows. Keep 2" to framing, supports and insulation.
Top vent kit / clean face (if used)
Use the Wilkening top vent kit and its 8" insulated aluminum duct. Clean face (CFK) also needs the dual top vent (TVK); its 8" ducts run down or sideways up to 6', never upward.

Top vent: 6" min from the top of the assembly to the finished ceiling; its bottom at least 6" above a combustible mantel and 6" above the unit top. Never create a heat trap; closeable top vents can't be used. A single top vent may be used with the front outlet; to seal the front vent, use dual top vents. Allow return air from remote areas.

Auxiliary heat distribution kit: from the 4" outlet at the back right, up to 12' in any direction; never set its grille in a floor.
Power & optional blower
Remove the magnetic lower grill, bring 110VAC, 10 amp power to the junction box per the National Electric Code, add the blower if used, reinstall the grill.

Blower mounts at the base center, 4" behind the lower grill, on the threaded studs with the wing nuts provided. Slide the heat sensor into the slotted bracket at the far right bottom of the front; keep wires off the steel. Wire nut all connections. Ground through the metal electrical box on the right behind the lower louver.
Install the doors
Apply the adhesive heat resistant gasket outside the predrilled holes around the opening and fix the frame with the 8 screws from the door carton. Wilkening door only; never operate without doors.

Door options (p. 19)Black Rectangular Tudor (part #GVBRT), Black Rectangular Prairie Style Tudor (part #GVBRTP), Black Arched Tudor (part #GVBAT), Nickel Rectangular Tudor (part #GVNRT), Nickel Arched Tudor (part #GVNAT), Single Black Rectangular (part #GVBRS)
Maker's website: Door options: Arched Black; Arched Ancient Iron; Arched Prairie; Rectangular Black; Rectangular Ancient Iron; Rectangular Prairie.
Facing & hearth finish
Combustibles flush to the face sides with a 3/8" gap; 4" Micore above the unit to the header. Attach facing kits to the framing, not tight to the face; caulk seams with 500 degree RTV silicone.

Combustible material may not project in front of or over the steel face; brick, stone or tile may cross it. Self-tapping screws into the steel front are allowed for a facing kit, but don't tighten them, or thermal expansion may crack the mortar. Create a tight seal between the steel face and the facing (typically the mortar scratch coat) so heat can't flow between them. Leave 3/8" between sheet rock and the unit sides.

Remove plated trim during installation; sheet rock compound discolors plated surfaces.
Liner, baffle, louver & handover
Install the upper steel baffle and the Skamol refractory liner, then the magnetic heat outlet louver if used. Leave the instructions inside the unit for the owner.

1. Steel baffle with holes on the tabs in the upper throat, above the secondary air tubes.
  2. Two upper side panels above the side air tube (part #6).
  3. Two bottom pieces (parts #1 and #2).
  4. Two-piece back panel (part #3), joined at the top center edge with the stainless "U" clip.
  5. Four side pieces (part #4), each front one before its back one.
  6. Panel #5 over the top edge of the air tubes, resting on the back panel.
  7. Two-piece refractory top baffle plate on the dual stainless air tubes.
Never operate without all baffles and the liner in place; the chimney connector and fireplace components can overheat.

panels.title: Back smoking when the doors open
items: Doors opened fast or one at a time → vortex at the opening; open both together, slowly
Excessive fuel → over capacity; wet fuel → low draft from low firebox temperature
Leaves, nest or heavy creosote in the flue → poor draw
Chimney less than 2' above any roof or structure within 10', or offsets without added height → poor draw

panels.title: Sudden smoking after normal operation
items: Loose creosote fallen down the chimney, blocking the holes in the uppermost baffle

panels.title: Air drops down the chimney
items: Negative pressure (stack effect) in a tight home: lower levels run lower pressure
Fix: close windows above, open one on the fireplace level; light crumpled newspaper, doors closed, air open
Exterior chimney in areas below 0° Fahrenheit → poor draft, creosote, slow starts
Basement unit with an outside chimney → flow reversal on start up

panels.title: Heavy smoke on the glass
items: Wet wood, too small a fire, or door closed too soon after lighting → firebox too cool
Combustion air closed while the fire burns
Large, un-split or tightly stacked wood

light.title: Starting a fire
light.html:
First open the combustion air: lift the lever at the lower left of the door frame and a spring opens it. Build the fire right on the base of the firebox; don't use a grate or andirons.

Owner's manual: a top-down fire

  1. Lay 2 large split logs on the base, cut ends pointing to each side.
  2. Add a row of smaller split wood on top, cut ends pointing to the back.
  3. On that, put crumpled newspaper or a fire starter, with fine kindling and several small split pieces over and around it.
  4. Light the starter and close the door. The fire burns from the top down; when the large logs are used up, add wood on top.

Installation manual: paper and kindling

Crumple 8-10 sheets of newspaper into balls in the center. Lay two small split logs on each side of the paper, cut ends facing you, and crisscross dry kindling on top. Light the paper and leave the door ajar for 8-10 minutes to get the chimney drawing. Add more kindling and close the doors. When that load is about half burned, add cord wood up to 4" in diameter, then larger wood once the fireplace is hot.

Note: the two manuals start a fire differently. The owner's manual builds the fire top-down and closes the door once it's lit (p. 2); the installation manual lights paper under the kindling and leaves the door ajar 8-10 minutes (pp. 20–21).

firstfire.title: Your first fires
firstfire.html:
The first fires break the fireplace in. Keep them small and short, less than one hour each, and don't burn fast-burning material like building scrap or siding. The owner's manual asks this of the first two to three fires (p. 2), the installation manual of the first two (p. 20). Make the very first fire especially short: it drives most of the moisture out of the refractory liner and heat-cures the gasket cement.

Odor and smoke are normal at first

For the first several fires you'll notice an odor and/or some smoke as the paint cures and oils burn off the outer metal. Keep the room well ventilated. People who are allergic to smoke or have asthma shouldn't be in the room during this curing.

Stained glass

While it cures, the glass may get creosote stains over the whole panel. These small fires aren't hot enough for the glass to clean itself.

air.title: The combustion air control
air.html:
Your GranView draws outside air for the fire, piped to every combustion air port. It's a single burn rate fireplace, so the air supply is either open or closed.

  • To open it, lift up on the lever at the lower left of the door frame. A spring opens the supply.
  • Keep it open whenever a fire is burning. If it isn't open, the fire dies and the glass gets badly smoked up. Closing it on a burning fire also builds up gases in the firebox.
  • When you're not using the fireplace, push the handle in and lock it in the notch on the lever. That stops air flowing in and chilling the steel and the room.
  • Never plug the outside air supply.
In a chimney fire, close it: push the air control in to its locked position, make sure the doors are fully closed, call the fire department, warn your family and get out.

refuel.title: Adding wood
refuel.html:
Keep the firebox hot: hold a hot bed of coals and don't stack or overload it with wood. A fire that runs cool smolders, smokes up the glass and builds creosote in the chimney.

When you add wood

  1. Crack the doors open for 15 seconds to clear any smoke. If you're opening both, crack them at the same time.
  2. Open them the rest of the way slowly and add wood. With a large, active fire you may want to open only the right-hand door, to cut the radiant heat on you.
  3. Place the wood crisscross so air can get under the fire, and keep it behind the log retainer so nothing burning spills out when the door opens.

What to burn

Only solid wood or processed solid fuel fire logs (use fire logs listed for fireplace use), with less than 20% moisture. Smaller split wood gives the most heat; large, un-split or tightly stacked wood burns slower and smokes the glass. Don't burn wood that sizzles. Never burn coal, charcoal, treated wood or wood that's been in saltwater, and don't load it with cardboard, paper or other fast-burning material.

Run it with both doors fully open or fully closed, never partly open. Cracking them open for a cold start or while refueling is allowed for up to 15 minutes.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
Some smoke on the glass is normal with any wood fire. After a series of fires the outer edges cloud over, usually in a band less than 2" wide on each edge, and won't burn clean in normal use.

If the glass smokes over in a low fire or at the end of one, start a large fire and let its heat burn the deposit off. Heavy smoke on the glass means the fire is running too cool: wet wood, too small a fire, or the door closed too soon after lighting.

To clean it

  • Wait until the fireplace has cooled to room temperature.
  • Use an ammonia based cleaner, a fireplace glass cleaner or Speedy White (from your dealer or Wilkening).
  • Wipe off the residue with a soft cotton cloth or paper towel. Never use razor blades or abrasive pads; they damage the glass and can make it fail.
  • Keep cleaner off painted and plated surfaces, which it can discolor. Cleaner mixed with creosote also hardens the gaskets.
The glass is 1400 degree ceramic glass. If it breaks, replace it only with the same kind from your dealer or Wilkening; regular or tempered glass can't take the heat. Replace cracked or broken glass before you use the fireplace again.

smoke.title: Smoke coming into the room
smoke.html:
Smoke rolling into the room when you open the doors is called back smoking. The usual causes:

  • Opening the doors too fast. Open both doors at the same time, slowly. That calms the swirl of air rushing in.
  • Too much wood, or wet wood. Too much fuel overwhelms it; wet fuel keeps the firebox too cool to draw well.
  • A blocked chimney: leaves, a nest, or too much creosote in the flue.
  • A chimney that's too short. It must be at least 2' taller than any roof or structure within 10'. Installations with offsets may need extra height; ask your dealer.

It was fine, then suddenly smoked

Check that the chimney cap isn't plugged and that loose creosote hasn't fallen down the chimney and blocked the holes in the uppermost baffle.

Cold air coming down the chimney

In a tight house the lower floors can have lower pressure. Close windows on the floors above the fireplace and open one on its level, ideally one the wind is blowing toward. To get it drawing, light a few crumpled sheets of newspaper with the doors closed and the air supply open.

chimney.title: Chimney care and creosote
chimney.html:
Burning wood gives off vapors and tar that condense in a cool flue as creosote, a black deposit that burns extremely hot if it ignites. Hot fires with well-seasoned, air dried wood keep it down. Don't burn wood that sizzles in the fire, or wood over 20% moisture.

How often

  • Inspect the chimney monthly and clean it if needed; at a minimum, inspect it twice each heating season.
  • Don't let more than 1/8 inch build up between cleanings.
  • Have a certified chimney sweep or your dealer inspect the system every year before the first fire, even if you clean it yourself.

Cleaning

Professional cleaning is recommended. If you do it yourself, take off the chimney cap and use a stiff plastic/poly brush; metal brushes scratch the stainless chimney. First take out the steel and refractory baffles in the throat and the angled refractory above the fire chamber so creosote falls to the base, then clear it out before the next fire.

Put all baffles and liner panels back before you burn. A hairline crack in a liner panel that stays in place is fine; replace a panel that falls loose or leaves gaps.

ash.title: Removing ashes
ash.html:
Take ashes out only when the fire is out and the ash is cold. Your dealer has a special ash bucket that makes the job easier.

  • Always empty ash into a metal container with a lid. Never use a cardboard box.
  • Close the lid tight and set the container on a noncombustible surface or the ground, well away from anything that can burn.
  • Don't store ash in your home.
  • If you bury the ashes or spread them, keep them in the closed container until all the cinders have cooled completely.
Ash stays dangerous: hot coals in the ash can remain dangerous for several days after you remove them.

safety.title: Safety and chimney fires
safety.html:
• Keep furniture and anything else that can burn at least 3 feet from the front of the fireplace.
  • Never leave children alone with a fire burning. Everyone who uses the fireplace should learn how it works first.
  • Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, lighter fluid or any liquid to start or freshen a fire. Keep all such liquids well away from the fireplace while it is in use.
  • No gas logs, gas starters, flame colorants, coal or charcoal.
  • Never block the air circulation grills (inlet or outlet); the structure can overheat.
  • Don't slam the doors, build the fire against the glass, or over-fire the fireplace.
  • Keep a multi-purpose fire extinguisher nearby. A smoke detector and a carbon monoxide (CO) detector in the room are recommended.
  • Let it cool, and shut off the electrical supply, before any service.

If you have a chimney fire

  1. Push the combustion air control in to its locked position.
  2. Make sure the doors are fully closed.
  3. Call the fire department, warn your family and get everyone out.

Don't use the fireplace again until a certified sweep or another qualified person has inspected the whole system.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
The GranView 10 Year Warranty covers the original retail purchaser, from the date of purchase. It can't be transferred to a later owner.

Door frame and all metal parts10 years
Control rods and knobs, gasket seals, electrical components, refractory liner1 year

A defective metal part

First yearrepaired or replaced at no cost
Years 2 to 5replacement part at no cost
Years 6 to 10replacement part at 50% of the current retail price

Labor, postage and freight aren't covered, and neither are parts made by others, such as painted or electroplated surfaces.

What voids it

  • Alterations, improper installation, abuse, neglect or over-firing.
  • No chimney cap. A cap must be installed.
  • Wilkening may void it if the unit is installed outside the continental United States or Canada, or moved from where it was first installed.
Send in the registration card: for the warranty to take effect, the completed owner's registration card must be returned to Wilkening within sixty (60) days of purchase.

specChimney.title: Chimney
specChimney.html:

Max offset30 degree · no more than two sets of 30 degree elbows
Clearance to combustibles2" min
Typical framing, 8" 2100 degree HT14 ½" x 14 ½"

Adapt with the chimney brand's anchor plate: 4 self tapping metal screws, sealed to the unit with 600 degree RTV silicone. Firestop and/or radiation shield at every combustible penetration except the roof (flashing or chase top); sealed storm collar at the flashing; roof support through the upper roof; roof brace if more than 6' is exposed above the roof. Keep a pipe section between elbows to ease cleaning. Chimney cap required on all installations to validate the warranty. Enclose the chimney in living areas. Never connect to a flue serving another appliance. Multiple flues in one chase: terminations 16" apart horizontally and 12" vertically (recommended).

specClear.html:

No framing above the unit except a front header supporting the face, no closer than the metal stand-off. Never install without the clearance spacers or with modified spacers; don't notch the header or framing. The unit may sit directly on wood flooring with all carpet or vinyl removed. Don't fill the required air spaces with insulation or any material; insulate between the stud walls behind the sheet rock.

For a combustible mantel 8" deep, measured above the base the fireplace sits on. With top vents, the bottom of the top vent must also be at least 6" above a combustible mantel and 6" above the unit top, with 6" from the top of the vent assembly to the finished ceiling (p. 9).

specHearth.html:

Single door option: carry noncombustible material past the door's foremost swing to contain embers riding the door's inner channel. Lay the first spark-guard section on the protruding hearth, then slide the second under the unit, overlapping the lower section's vertical return. No spark guard is needed on a non-combustible base with no combustibles below the hearth. Outside the Micore area, hearth materials may contact combustibles. Don't obstruct the room air inlet at the unit base.

conflicts.issue: Fire-starting method differs. Owner's manual: top-down lay (2 large split logs, a row of smaller split wood, then newspaper or a fire starter with kindling on top), light and close the door. Installation manual: 8-10 crumpled sheets of newspaper in the center with small split logs on each side and kindling on top, door left ajar 8-10 minutes, then closed. (Doc 2 p. 3 also lists closing the door too soon after lighting as a cause of low temperatures.)
Number of small, short break-in fires: 'the first two to three fires' in the owner's manual vs 'the first two fires' in the installation manual.
conflicts.reason: 'Two to three' (owner's manual) is a range that starts at the installation manual's 'two'; both pages say to keep these first fires small and short (less than one hour), so two or three such fires satisfy both. The drawer now states both counts with their pages.
